Reductive Cross-Coupling of Alcohol Derivatives with Chlorosilanes
via Pyridines-Promoted Si─Cl Activation
Changpeng Chen+, Tenggang Jiao+, Zhitao Zhang, Xiaoming Zeng,* and Xuefeng Cong*
Abstract: The development of efficient approaches medi-
ated by silyl radicals for constructing C─Si bonds is of
great interest and importance, yet methods to generate
these intermediates from readily available chlorosilanes
remain scarce. Herein, we report a new strategy for
silyl radical generation via pyridines-promoted reductive
Si─Cl activation of chlorosilanes and demonstrate its
application in the reductive cross-coupling with a wide
array of benzyl, allyl, and propargyl alcohol derivatives.
This protocol offers an efficient and step-economical
route for the synthesis of diverse benzyl-, allyl-, and
allenylsilanes, featuring broad substrate scope and easy
scalability. Mechanistic investigations suggest that the
coupling reaction was initiated by the reductive Si─Cl
activation of chlorosilanes with magnesium promoted by
pyridine derivatives, which generates silyl radicals. These
silyl radicals subsequently mediate the deoxygenation of
alcohol derivatives to form carbon radicals, culminating
in C─Si radical–radical cross-coupling.
Introduction
Organosilicon compounds have broad applications in many
research fields of modern chemistry. In particular, benzyl-,
allyl-, and allenylsilanes serve as versatile building blocks in
synthetic chemistry and material science due to their diverse
reactivity.<sup>[1–12]</sup> Therefore, the development of an efficient
and general strategy for the synthesis of these organosilicon
compounds is of great interest and much importance. Cross-
coupling reactions with silicon reagents have emerged as one
of the most attractive and powerful strategies for construct-
ing silicon-containing molecules.<sup>[13–18]</sup> Remarkable advances
have recently been made to develop cross-coupling of carbon
electrophiles with diverse silicon nucleophiles by transition
metal catalysts, greatly expanding access to functionalized
organosilanes.<sup>[19–36]</sup> However, the reductive cross-coupling of
carbon electrophiles with silicon electrophiles has remained
underdeveloped to date. Given the diversity and abundance
of both carbon electrophiles and silicon electrophiles, devel-
oping an efficient and general strategy for the reductive
cross-coupling of these two bench-stable electrophiles to
access organosilanes such as benzyl-, allyl-, and allenylsilanes
is of great interest and importance.(Supporting Information)
Chlorosilanes are among the most accessible feedstock
chemical in organosilicon chemistry. Recently, transition-
metal-catalyzed reductive cross-coupling reactions of
chlorosilanes have become a powerful tool for the C─Si
bond formation,<sup>[37–40]</sup> and the coupling reactions with
various carbon electrophiles have been achieved.<sup>[37–52]</sup> These
coupling reactions are facilitated by oxidative addition
of a Si─Cl bond to a low-valent metal center to form a
silametalated intermediate (Scheme 1a). Alternatively, the
direct generation of a silyl radical by means of the reductive
activation of chlorosilanes followed by coupling with a carbon
electrophile or radical is a synthetically appealing strategy
for the construction of C─Si bonds. However, such coupling
reaction remains rarely studied due to the challenging single-
electron reduction of the strong Si─Cl bonds. Recently, Lin
and coworkers developed an electro reductive approach
to access silyl radicals by activating chlorosilanes with
attractive applications in coupling with various alkenes for
the formation of the C─Si bonds.<sup>[53,54]</sup> Herein, we report a
new and alternative method for generating silyl radicals via
the reductive activation of chlorosilanes with magnesium
promoted by pyridine derivatives and demonstrate its
attractive application in the reductive cross-coupling with a

alcohol derivatives with chlorosilanes without the need for
transition-metal-catalysts, offering an efficient and step-
economical route for the synthesis of diverse benzyl-, allyl-,
and allenylsilanes.

Results and Discussion
At first, we examined the cross-coupling reaction of 2-
naphthylmethyl methyl ether 1a with chlorotrimethylsilane 2a
by using 99.99% purity magnesium as the reductant (Table 1).
When the reaction was carried out in THF at 80 °C, no
significant reaction between 1a and 2a was observed (Table 1,
entry 1). To our delight, addition of a catalytic amount of 2,2--
bipyridine (5 mol%) into the reaction dramatically promoted
the reaction, affording the cross-coupling product 3a in 59%
yield (Table 1, entry 2). The replacement of 2,2--bipyridine
by 4,4--dimethyl-2,2--bipyridyl further increased the yield of
coupling product 3a to 72% (Table 1, entry 3), whereas 4,4--
dimethoxyl-2,2--dipyridyl showed a slightly lower reactivity
(Table 1, entry 4). The use of 4,4--di-tert-butyl-2,2--dipyridyl
(dtbpy) remarkably increased the reactivity to afford the
desired coupling product 3a in 90% yield (Table 1, entry 5). In
contrast, 6,6--di-methyl-2,2--dipyridyl and o-phenanthroline
showed much less efficiency in promoting the cross-coupling
of 1a with 2a (Table 1, entries 6 and 7). It was worth noting
that various pyridines such as pyridine, 2-methylpyridine
and 2,6-dimethylpyridine are also effective for the present
coupling reaction with slightly diminished yields (Table 1,
entries 8–10). In the presence of a catalytic amount of
dtbpy (5 mol%), decreasing the amount of magnesium from
2.0 equiv. to 1.0 equiv. lowered the product yield to 50%
(Table 1, entry 11). No significant reaction between 1a and
2a was observed in the absence of a magnesium reductant
(Table 1, entry 12). Subsequently, the coupling reaction of
other 2-naphthalenylmethyl alcohol derivatives with 2a was
examined. The reaction of 2-naphthalenylmethyl acetate 1b
with 2a showed a similar performance with that of 1a, giving
the desired coupling product 3a in 75% yield in the presence
of dtbpy (5 mol%) but no product 3a in the absence of dtbpy
(5 mol%) (Table 1, entries 13 and 14). In the reaction of
2-naphthylmethyl 2-pyridyl ether 1c with 2a, the absence of
dtbpy did not influence the reactivity, affording the coupling
product 3a in 90% yield (Table 1, entries 15 and 16). These
results indicated that the pyridine unit played a critically
important role in promoting the cross-coupling reaction of
2-naphthylmethyl alcohol derivatives with 2a.

Although more studies are required to establish a precise
mechanism, based on the above experimental results and
previous reports,<sup>[61–64]</sup> possible mechanisms for the reductive
cross-coupling reactions of benzyl methyl ether 1a, cinnamyl
methyl ether 4a, and propargyl methyl ether 6a with 2a in
the presence of dtbpy are proposed as shown in Scheme 4.
The combination of 2a and dtbpy would form a siliconium-
chloride salt,<sup>[65–67]</sup> which undergoes reductive activation with
magnesium to generate a dtbpy-coordinated silyl radical. The
subsequent deoxygenation of 1a and 4a by the resulting silyl
radical would yield the corresponding benzyl and allyl radical,
respectively.<sup>[68]</sup> The C─Si radical coupling of the benzyl and
allyl radical with the silyl radical would give the desired
products 3a and 5a, respectively, and release dtbpy. In the
case of propargyl methyl ether 6a, the deoxygenation with the
silyl radical would yield a propargyl radical and its resonance
hybrid allenyl radical. The allenyl–silyl radical coupling would
selectively take place due to the steric reason, giving the
allenylsilane 7a. It should be noted that, although silyl radical
formation was unambiguously established, a competing silyl
anion pathway cannot be fully excluded.
Conclusion
In summary, we have developed a pyridines-promoted strat-
egy for the reductive Si─Cl activation of readily available
chlorosilanes and demonstrated its attractive application in
the reductive cross-coupling with a wide array of benzyl,
allyl, and propargyl alcohol derivatives under simple and
transition-metal-free conditions. Mechanistic studies revealed
that the coupling reaction proceeded through the generation
of silyl radicals via pyridines-promoted reductive activation
of the strong Si–Cl bond of chlorosilanes with magnesium
followed by the deoxygenation of alcohol derivatives by
the resulting silyl radicals to form carbon radicals and
subsequent C–Si radical-radical cross-coupling. This work not
only constitutes an efficient and step-economical protocol for
the synthesis of diverse benzyl-, allyl,- and allenylsilanes but
also offers a new and general strategy for developing new
silyl radical chemistry. Further studies on transformations
of chlorosilanes via the reductive activation of strong Si─Cl
bonds are in progress.
